The Amṛtabindu Upaniṣad.
"May He protect us both"—this is the Peace invocation.
The mind alone is the cause of bondage and liberation.
The mind is indeed said to be of two kinds: pure and impure.
The impure is characterized by desire and volition; the pure is devoid of desire. || 1 ||
The mind alone is the cause of bondage and liberation for human beings;
attached to sense objects, it leads to bondage, while free from sense objects, it is known to lead to liberation. (2)
That supreme nectar which is known through the *Amṛtabindu Upaniṣad*—
that indeed is the one called Tripādrāmacandra, our ultimate refuge.

Now, indeed, this *Amṛtabindu Upaniṣad* is a division of the *Kṛṣṇayajurveda*. Its introductory context and thematic connection are similar to those of the *Kaṭhavallī* and other texts. This [Upaniṣad] proceeds in a distinct form without a narrative frame (*ākhyāyikā*). A commentary on it is begun here due to its brevity. Regarding the word "mind" (*mana*): the mind is that very principle of *māyā* which performs the mentalizing (*manana*) that "there exists something separate from itself," by one whose vision is that of the ignorant—[a vision] established through the negation (*apahnava*) of the state of ignorance and its effects as something separate from oneself, and which is the non-dual Brahman alone. By the word "indeed" (*hi*), the fact that the mind composed of the three qualities (*guṇa*) is of the nature of absolute non-existence (*niṣpratiyogikābhāva*) is illuminated. The mind, imagined as if real by the vision of one’s own ignorance, is of two kinds.

(27) This has been declared according to the scriptures. As for the question of what its two forms are: "Its sattva aspect is pure, and its rajas-tamas aspect is indeed impure. The scripture itself explains these two terms; it clarifies that the "impure" is characterized by desire and volition because it is a portion of ignorance (avidyā), while that which is devoid of general desire is "pure" because it is a portion of knowledge (vidyā). || 1 || It is said that the mind alone is the cause of bondage and liberation: "The mind alone. The mind possessing functions such as volition is the cause of bondage; the mind free from volition is the cause of liberation—this is the meaning. || 2 ||
The cessation of the mind is the means to liberation, since liberation is desired for this mind when it is devoid of objects;
therefore, the seeker of liberation must constantly render the mind objectless. (3)
When the mind, with its attachment to sense objects cast aside, is completely restrained within the heart and reaches a state of self-absorption,
that is the supreme state.
It should be restrained right then and there until it reaches dissolution within the heart;
this alone is knowledge and meditation, while all else is merely an elaborate system of logic.

Since the state of the mind being devoid of objects is the cause of liberation, [the author] says "yataḥ" (since), implying that one who desires liberation must make the mind objectless. || 3 || He states that the very state of becoming "mindless" (*amanībhāva*) is liberation: "nirasta... etc. When the mind—whose attachment to objects has been dispelled through meditation on Brahman—is completely restrained within the heart, and at whatever time it attains its own non-existence, that is, the state of being "mindless," then at that time, that supreme state which is established through the negation of everything else remains as Brahman alone, free from all opposition. || 4 || He declares that the realization that Brahman is established through the negation of the mind and its effects is indeed *jñāna* (knowledge); this is the ultimate purport of all Vedānta: "tāvat... etc. As long as the mind, possessing fluctuations such as desire, has not reached dissolution within the heart, so long must the mind be restrained. That which knows Brahman—which is established through the negation of the mind and its effects—to be nothing but itself (*svamātra*) is this non-dual knowledge and meditation. Through these two terms, one is to know and meditate upon Brahman as being nothing but oneself, free from all opposition.

It is illuminated that [nothing else] can be known or meditated upon as distinct from itself, because Brahman alone is without a counter-correlative (niṣpratiyogika). Beyond that, all remaining logic and elaboration are merely a beginning in speech (vācārambhaṇamātra), according to the Śruti: "Modification is a mere name, a beginning in speech. || 5 ||
Through the knowledge of Brahman, the attainment of the state of Brahman occurs;
it is neither conceivable nor inconceivable, yet it is both inconceivable and indeed conceivable. When one is completely free from partiality, then one attains Brahman.

The text states that for one who knows the true nature of Brahman, there is the attainment of its very being—expressed by the words "not at all" (naiva). This [Brahman] is not to be thought of as something separate from oneself, because it is one's own self alone (svamātra). Nor is it unthinkable as one's own self; it is not to be thought of as having attributes (saviśeṣa), yet it is indeed to be thought of as being "one's very self. When one knows that Brahman is free from such partiality (pakṣapāta)—falling into the positions of "not to be thought of" and so forth—and realizes that Brahman is one's own self alone, then at the very moment of that realization, one attains Brahman; the meaning is that one becomes Brahman itself. || 6 ||
Through the contemplation of Brahman with attributes, one attains Brahman without attributes.
One should unite yoga by means of sound and contemplate the soundless;
through the experience of the soundless, non-existence is not intended as existence. (7)
That very Brahman is partless, free from conceptual construction, and stainless;
having realized "I am that Brahman," one certainly attains Brahman. (8)
That which is free from conceptual construction, infinite, devoid of causes and examples, immeasurable, and beginningless—by knowing this, the wise one is liberated. || 9 ||
There is neither cessation nor arising, neither one bound nor one who practices, neither one desiring liberation nor one liberated—this is the ultimate reality. (10)

He says that the realization of the attributeless Brahman (*nirviśeṣa-brahma*) may occur through the meditation on the Brahman with attributes (*saviśeṣa-brahmopāsanā*): "By means of sound" (*svareṇa*). By means of the sound of *Oṃ*, one should first effect a union with the lower Brahman (*apara-brahma*), performing the contemplation: "I am the Lord with attributes. Through the grace of the Brahman with attributes, one should contemplate the supreme, soundless (*asvara*), attributeless Brahman. The connection with the preceding is: by means of the soundless, attributeless Brahman, through its manifestation (*anubhāvena*), one should contemplate the supreme Brahman itself as being soundless. If it is argued that "soundless" (*asvara*) means the absence of sound, no; for the soundless is the attributeless Brahman and is thus of the nature of an existent reality (*bhāva-rūpa*). Indeed, an existent reality is never intended to be a non-existence (*abhāva*). || 7 || Since this is so, therefore, that which is indeed soundless is the partless Brahman (*niṣkala*), because it is augmented by being distinct from the sixteen digits (*kalā*) beginning with breath and ending with name; it is free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*) because of the impossibility of conceptual constructions imagined by itself; and it is stainless (*nirañjana*) due to the absence of anything other than itself that could serve as a stain. Knowing "I am that Brahman," at the very moment of that knowledge, one attains the eternal, attributeless Brahman. || 8 || He states the same meaning in a different manner: "Free from conceptual construction" (*nirvikalpam*). That wherein the fourteen or fifteen conceptual constructions—beginning with the waking-of-waking state and ending with the single-flavor of permission (*anujñaikarasa*)—culminate as nothing but themselves, that is "free from conceptual construction. One might think that the attributeless, being subtle, must have an end; therefore he says: "and infinite" (*anantaṃ ca*). This is because of the absence of the three kinds of limitation; for the Śruti says: "Brahman is devoid of limitation in space, time, and substance. The word "and" (*ca*) indicates an infinity that has no counter-correlative (*niṣpratiyogika*). What is the reason or what is the illustration for this stated meaning? To this he says: "devoid of cause and illustration" (*hetudṛṣṭāntavarjitam*). Because there is no cause other than itself for its own establishment, and because an illustration is impossible since it is without a counter-correlative. Since this is so, it is "unmeasurable" (*aprameya*), because it cannot be sustained by any means of knowledge other than the Vedānta. Even if it is unmeasurable, one might think it has a beginning; therefore he says: "and without beginning" (*anādiṃ ca*). For in the case of the absolute Being (*sanmātra*) which has no counter-correlative, origination and so forth are impossible. By the word "and," the unborn nature of even that which appears to be other than itself is indicated, according to the Śruti: "One sees here also only Being, and the rest is non-existent; Brahman alone is, not the non-existent. Having known this, the wise man, at the very moment of knowledge, is liberated from the delusion of the existence of anything other than himself; the meaning is that only his own Self remains. || 9 ||

(30) Having raised the objection, "Since the established order of origination, dissolution, bondage, liberation, and so forth is observed, how can there be the realization of one's own nature alone? [the author] replies that because this [order] is imagined by one's own ignorance (*svāvidyā*), it is equal to its cause; therefore, the realization of one's own nature alone is unrestricted and without a counter-correlate (*niṣpratiyogika*). Thus he says: "There is no cessation" (*na nirodha*). "Cessation" (*nirodha*) means dissolution (*pralaya*); "origination" (*utpatti*) means birth (*jāti*); "the bound" (*baddha*) is the transmigrating being (*saṃsārī*); "the seeker of liberation" (*mumukṣu*) is the knower (*pramātā*) who desires to be freed from his own ignorance and its effects; and "the liberated" (*mukta*) is one whose bonds of worldly existence have been severed. Since such conceptualizations arise from the appearance of existence as something other than oneself, and since any generality other than oneself is unreal—like the horn of a hare—and is thus of the nature of ignorance (*avidyā*), the origination, dissolution, and so forth of anything other than oneself are of the nature of absolute non-existence (*niṣpratiyogikābhāva*). In this regard, according to the statement of Paramākṣara: "Māyā, avidyā, jñāna, viśva, abhāva, antaḥkaraṇa, and so forth—all these synonyms for what is other than Brahman are of the nature of absolute non-existence. Therefore, cessation and the rest do not exist in one's own nature alone; this alone is the ultimate reality (*paramārthatā*). Consequently, the meaning is that the realization of Brahman alone, which is without a counter-correlate, is unrestricted. || 10 ||
One should consider the self as a single unity; the self is indeed one throughout the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep.
For that which has transcended these three states, rebirth no longer exists.
For the single Self of all beings, residing in every being,
is seen as one and also as many, like the moon reflected in water.

One might argue that there would be a difference in the perception of that [Self] due to the differences in its states; therefore, he says: "It is one. The division that occurs within the fourfold states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep—distinguished as Viśva-Viśva, etc., up to Anujñaikarasa and Avikalpa—should be understood as this Self being truly one alone. This is because the consciousness of the Viśva-Viśva and so forth, which persists through the various states such as waking-waking, is one, just as the space pervading a jar, a bowl, and other vessels is one. Thus, for one who has transcended the three states divided fourfold each time and has ascended to the fourth state (*turya*), there is no further rebirth in the form of Viśva-Viśva and so on, because the ignorance that is the cause of birth has been eliminated. (11) Furthermore, how is the oneness of the Self established? To this, he states its oneness with an illustration: "It is one. Indeed, the Self, though situated within the five elements and their derivatives, remains one alone. Depending on the perspectives of the individual self (*svajña*) and others, it appears as one or as many—like the moon appearing as a reflection in water while remaining the sky itself—due to the distinction between Śiva and the individual soul (*jīva*); yet in reality, the Self is one. (12)
The Self is devoid of birth and destruction;
just as when a jar containing space is being carried away, the jar may perish but the space does not, so too is the individual soul (jīva) comparable to space. (13)
Like a jar, it is repeatedly broken into various forms; yet while it does not know that breaking apart, it knows eternally.

One might think that because the Self is delimited by all its adjuncts (*upādhi*), its existence and non-existence would entail its own persistence and destruction. To this he says: "Like a jar" (*ghaṭa*). Just as the space enclosed within a jar (*ghaṭasaṃvṛtam*)—that is, the space delimited by a jar—appears to be carried away when the jar is moved elsewhere, yet it is not so in reality because space is immovable; and when the jar is destroyed, the space delimited by it does not likewise perish—so too, the individual soul (*jīva*), which is like space, neither moves nor perishes through the movement or destruction of its own adjuncts. This is according to the Śruti: "Verily, it is only when the soul has departed that this [body] dies; the soul does not die. (13) He says: "Like a jar" (*ghaṭavat*), to show that he alone knows the true nature of the Self who understands how the Self appears or does not appear depending on the existence or non-existence of its own adjuncts. Just as a jar and other objects have various forms, so too the space delimited by them appears again and again to have various forms corresponding to the emerging shapes of jars and the like. When those jars and other objects are divided or destroyed, the common person does not perceive a division in the space delimited by them, but sees only undivided space. One who knows the true nature of that [Self], however, always perceives only the undivided space, regardless of the existence or non-existence of adjuncts such as jars. (14)
One who is veiled by the illusion of words does not perceive the unconditioned Self through darkness, even as it resides in the lotus of the heart;
but when that darkness is shattered, one perceives oneness alone.

(32) Likewise, one with the vision of ignorance perceives the manifold diversity of selves that conforms to limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*); yet, upon the removal of those adjuncts, one does not perceive such diversity. However, one whose intellect is fixed on the ultimate reality perceives the Self as truly one and without adjuncts, regardless of whether adjuncts exist or do not exist. This is stated [in the verse] beginning with *śabda*: The "illusion of sound" (*śabdamāyā*) is that which is the cause of the phenomenal expansion of words and their meanings; or rather, it is Māyā, which—being devoid of objective reality—is essentially mere sound, consisting of the "commencement of speech" (*vācārambhaṇa*), and is exceedingly skillful at effecting the impossible. A living being enveloped by this [Māyā] does not reach its own Self, which is supremely pure like a lotus (*puṣkara*), just as a being enveloped by darkness [does not see]. When the darkness of one's own ignorance is pierced by the light of self-knowledge—just as darkness is dispelled by a lamp—and when, by the word "and" (*ca*), the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of that [ignorance] have perished, one perceives the oneness of the inward and outward consciousness. Alternatively: One who is ignorant of the Self, being enveloped by the illusion of sound, does not attain the knowledge of the identity of all beings with the inward Brahman, just as a being enveloped by darkness [does not see] the lotus. But one who knows the Self, once the darkness of his own ignorance is pierced, perceives the oneness of all beings with the inward [Self] within the Supreme Self, which is like a lotus. However, the vision of ultimate reality perceives the essence of Brahman—which cannot tolerate any division between the inward and the outward—as being nothing but one’s own Self, free from all counter-correlates. || 15 ||
Through meditation on the Word-Brahman (śabdabrahman), one attains the Supreme Brahman;

the syllable of sound is the Supreme Brahman, and when that has ceased, there is the Imperishable (akṣara). If one desires peace for oneself, one should meditate upon that Imperishable known by the wise. (16)
Two kinds of knowledge are to be known: that which is the Brahman of Sound and that which is the Supreme Brahman.
One who is well-versed in the Brahman of Sound attains the Supreme Brahman. (17)
Having studied the scriptures, the wise man, intent upon knowledge and realization, should discard the scriptures entirely, just as one seeking grain discards the straw. || 18 ||

He states the means for realizing Brahman alone, which is without distinctions: "The syllable," etc. That syllable *oṃ*, known as the supreme support of Brahman as the means for attaining the undifferentiated Brahman, is the syllable of sound (*śabdākṣara*). When that [syllable], having parts, is exhausted—that is, when it has undergone dissolution—there remains the imperishable substratum of the dissolution of the syllable of sound, which does not decay. If the wise one desires the cessation of the phenomenal world of perishable and imperishable things as something separate from himself, then he should realize that supreme imperishable (*paramākṣara*), which is established through the negation of all discardable portions pertaining to both the perishable and the imperishable, consisting of the supported and the support. That is this imperishable.

"One should meditate on 'I am That'. (16) He says "Two" to show that through the knowledge of the true nature of the Śabda-Brahman (the Brahman as Word), preceded by the rejection of the phenomenal expansion of sound (*śabda-prapañca*), there occurs the realization of the Brahman which is its meaning (*tad-artha-brahma*). There are two kinds of Brahman—the Śabda-Brahman and the Para-Brahman. Regarding these two, the Śabda-Brahman and the Para-Brahman, two types of knowledge (*vidyā*) are to be known; that is, the true nature of the Brahman with attributes (*saguṇa*) and the Brahman without attributes (*nirguṇa*) must be understood. The word "tu" (but/and) is for the purpose of emphasis. Because these two consist of the means (*upāya*) and the goal (*upeya*), the sage who is proficient in the Śabda-Brahman—which is the Brahman with attributes—attains the knowledge of the Nirviśeṣa-Brahman (Brahman without attributes) through constant contemplation (*anusandhāna*) of the Brahman signified by the *praṇava* (Om). Simultaneous with the arising of that knowledge, he realizes the Supreme Brahman as being solely his own self, established by the total negation (*apahnava*) of everything other than himself, free from all opposition. The meaning is that the knower remains as that alone. (17) Even when Brahman is realized, the study of the texts that are the cause of that realization should be performed. To this end, he says "The text": A wise person endowed with the fourfold qualifications (*sādhana-catuṣṭaya*), until the knowledge of Brahman alone arises, should be intent upon that knowledge and realization. Having studied the entire collection of Vedānta texts and having performed *śravaṇa* (listening) from the mouth of a guru until the five defects such as doubt are pacified, if then perfect knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*) born of *manana* (reflection) and *nididhyāsana* (meditation) arises, then he should discard the collection of texts entirely, like one seeking grain discards the straw, because they have served their purpose. Just as one who has reached the far shore of a river no longer requires a boat, so it is here. (18)
The inner self of all beings is one, just as the milk of cows of many colors has but a single color.
Knowledge perceives [the Self] like the milk, whereas the possessor of the marks [perceives it] as one does the individual cows. (19)
Like clarified butter hidden within milk, consciousness dwells within every single being;
it must be constantly churned within the mind by means of that which has become the churning-stick of the mind.

Lest it be argued that there would be a multiplicity of the inner self (pratyak) as delimited by various internal organs (antaḥkaraṇa), he says: "Like cows. Just as the milk of cows, though characterized by various colors, is of a single nature, so too the knowledge of the inner self (pratyag-jñāna), which conforms to various limiting adjuncts (liṅga), is of a single nature.

The word *tu* (but/however) is for the purpose of emphasis. (p. 34) [Objection: If this is so, why does the oneness of the Inner Self (*pratyañ*) of all beings not manifest? To this he says: "Like clarified butter" (*ghṛtamiva*). Just as clarified butter hidden in milk becomes manifest through churning and other means, so too the reality of the Inner Self (*pratyaktattva*), although it is the illuminator of the existence and non-existence of the modifications (*vṛtti*) of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) in every single being, dwells hidden from the vision of those ignorant of themselves (*svājña*). The word *ca* (and) is for the purpose of removing doubt. When the mind has turned toward the Inner Self, one must churn with that very mind which has become the churning-stick and attained the state of the Inner Self. The meaning is that through such continuous meditation, Brahman alone—which is established by the negation of the portion to be discarded within the unity of the distinction between the outward-facing (*parāk*) and the inward-facing (*pratyak*)—becomes manifest as being without a counterpart (*niṣpratiyogikatayā*). || 20 ||
Meditation is the means for the direct realization of that [Brahman];
having fixed the eye of knowledge through concentration, one should extract the Supreme like fire—partless, immovable, and tranquil. That is remembered as "I am Brahman. (21)
That which is the abode of all beings and which dwells within all beings as their benefactor— that I am, Vāsudeva.
Therefore, I am Vāsudeva; this is the Upaniṣad.

To the question, "How can Brahman, which is hidden from all beings, be directly realized? he says: *jñāna* (knowledge), etc. Knowledge alone, whose scope is the Brahman established by the negation of everything else (*sarvāpahnavasiddha*), is the "eye" (*netra*). Having fixed and placed this "eye of knowledge" within the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—the word "and" (*ca*) indicating that it cannot be accomplished by means other than knowledge—one should "extract" the supreme Brahman, which is free of all counterparts (*niṣpratiyogika*), like fire manifested by the friction of two pieces of wood. To the question, "While the constituents such as the vital breath (*prāṇa*) still exist, how can there be freedom from counterparts? he says: *niṣkala* (partless). This is because the establishment of Brahman alone is preceded by the negation of the sixteen constituents, beginning with the vital breath and ending with the name. Because it is complete (*pūrṇa*), it is immovable (*niścala*) and tranquil of anything other than itself; that which remains is remembered as Brahman characterized by these three terms—*niṣkala*, etc.—meaning that Brahman culminates in being one's own self alone. Manifesting the state of being the Self of all through the support of the half-measure (*ardhamātrā*) and the three parts of the partless Brahman, and showing its actual establishment as the Self alone, he concludes with: *sarva*, etc. That which is the abode (*adhivāsa*) or place of all beings because it is their substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*), that which dwells within beings as their inner ruler (*antaryāmin*), and that which [remains] as the benefactor of all...

(p. 35) That which remains as the immutable pure consciousness—that am I, Vāsudeva; that is Brahman known as the supreme Vāsudeva. He is called *Vāsu* because he dwells (*vasana*) within that which is other than himself; and he is called *deva* because he shines (*dīvyati*) as the Supreme Self, established as the non-dual Brahman alone through the negation of all removable aspects residing in the substratum—which is dependent upon the object to be presided over. Thus, the ultimate meaning is that nothing but his own self remains. The repetition [of the word] is for the sake of emphasis. The word "iti" and the term "Upaniṣad" signify the conclusion of the present Upaniṣad. || 22 ||
This clear commentary on the Bindūpaniṣad was written by Upadeśabrahmayogin, the disciple of Śrī Vāsudevendra. This work,
which is an exposition of the present Upaniṣad, consists of one hundred and thirty verses.
Thus ends the commentary on the Amṛtabindu Upaniṣad, completing the twentieth [treatise] in the exposition of the scripture of the one hundred and eight Upaniṣads beginning with the Śrīmad Īśa.
